title: EF1 existence for arbitrary mixed-item utilities
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
formal: For every integer \(n\ge 3\), every finite item set M and every profile of utility functions \(u_{i}:2^{M}\to \mathbb{R}\) with \(u_{i}(\varnothing )=0\), does there exist a complete allocation \(A=(A_{1},\ldots ,A_{n})\) such that for every ordered pair of agents i,j there is a set \(X\subseteq A_{i}\cup A_{j}\) with |\(X|\le 1\) satisfying \(u_{i}(A_{i}\setminus X)\ge u_{i}(A_{j}\setminus X)\)?
why: Tests whether one-item envy relief remains possible when item values have unrestricted interactions and may change sign across bundles. A positive answer would extend a basic fairness guarantee far beyond additive goods and chores; a negative answer would identify a limit of that guarantee itself.
status_note: Survey v4 question and definitions checked, with subsequent-work searches through 11 September 2026. The relevant AAAI 2026 work concerns a weaker two-removal guarantee and restricted valuation signs. No resolution of the general EF1 existence question was located; no exhaustive literature or independent proof audit is claimed.

progress.text: The extended survey states Open Question 1 for at least three agents with arbitrary utilities, noting that even identical arbitrary utilities remain unsettled in that source.

Bilò, Loebl and Vinci establish existence for the weaker up-to-one-good-and-one-chore comparison under sign-restricted valuations. The stated model and guarantee do not resolve unrestricted one-item EF1.

sentences: Agents divide a finite set of indivisible items, and each agent may assign an arbitrary real utility to every bundle.
The question asks whether a complete EF1 allocation always exists for three or more agents.
For each envy comparison, EF1 permits ignoring at most one item from either the envious agent’s own bundle or the other bundle.
An item’s effect may depend on its companions, so the model does not assume a fixed division into goods and chores.
The 2026 existence results allowing one removal from each bundle do not settle this stricter one-item question.

references.title: Mixed Fair Division: A Survey
references.authors: Shengxin Liu; Xinhang Lu; Mashbat Suzuki; Toby Walsh

definitions: The n agents are indexed by \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}\). Each utility is an arbitrary real-valued function on all subsets of the finite set M, normalized only at the empty set; no additivity, monotonicity, submodularity, common ranking or identical-utilities assumption is imposed. A complete allocation is an ordered partition of M into n pairwise disjoint bundles, with empty bundles allowed. An agent i envies j when \(u_{i}(A_{i})<u_{i}(A_{j})\). The displayed condition is envy-freeness up to one item \((\mathrm{EF}1)\) for mixed items. If there is no envy, \(X=\varnothing\) works. Otherwise one may hypothetically remove one item from i’s bundle or one item from j’s bundle, and compare both remaining bundles using i’s utility. Removing one item from both bundles simultaneously is not permitted. The choice of X may depend on i,j and the whole allocation. These removals only define the fairness comparison; no item is discarded or transferred from the complete allocation. Items have no required permanent designation as goods or chores, since an item’s marginal utility may depend on the surrounding bundle. The question concerns existence and imposes no input encoding, value-query bound or running-time requirement.
answer_criterion: Prove EF1 existence for every \(n\ge 3\) and every normalized arbitrary utility profile on a finite item set, or give a finite profile and prove that every complete allocation violates the displayed inequality for some ordered pair, for every allowed one-item removal. An impossibility result for a stronger fairness notion does not refute EF1, and an existence theorem permitting two removed items does not establish it.

context_blocks.title: Why either bundle can supply the removed item
context_blocks.text: With desirable goods, envy can disappear after ignoring a valuable item held by someone else. With burdens, it can disappear after ignoring a costly item in the envious agent’s own bundle. For example, if i values her bundle at −4 and j’s at 2, and deleting one item from her own bundle raises its value to 2, that comparison satisfies EF1.

context_blocks.title: One item can change character
context_blocks.text: An arbitrary utility can satisfy \(u(\{a\})=u(\{b\})=1\) but \(u(\{a,b\})=- 3\). Each item is beneficial when received alone and harmful when added to the other. This is allowed by the question, so a fixed classification of every item as a good or chore would restrict the model.

context_blocks.title: What was known in the survey
context_blocks.text: The survey records EF1 existence for two agents with arbitrary utilities and for any number of agents under additive or doubly-monotonic utilities. Doubly-monotonic means that, for each agent, every item has a fixed nonnegative or nonpositive marginal effect in every bundle. Open Question 1 removes that restriction for three or more agents.

context_blocks.title: One removal versus two
context_blocks.text: The AAAI 2026 paper proves related existence statements for a relaxation allowing one removal from each compared bundle, for nonnegative or nonpositive valuations. That may remove two items in a comparison. The present target allows at most one item in total and permits arbitrary real utility values.
